column4: This is Theo. Theo moved to Crumb Island three months ago. And the longest conversation he's had since then... was with a seagull.
Morning!
This is Ana. Starting today, Ana is going to say hello to Theo. Once a day. For thirty days.
No speeches. No fixing him. Just one hello. Oh, and keep an eye on that calendar on Theo's wall. Because on day thirty, something happens that neither of them sees coming.
About half of adults in the US say they experience loneliness. If that's you, nothing is broken. Loneliness works a lot like hunger. It's a signal that you need something. In this case, people.
Day one.
Hi! I'm Ana.
Nothing. He doesn't even look up.
But here's what researchers think is going on inside Theo. When you've been lonely for a while, your brain can get extra alert to rejection. Like a smoke alarm that's a little too sensitive.
So a friendly hello can feel risky. From the outside, it looks cold. From the inside, it's protection.
Day two. A nod. A tiny one. We're counting it.
Day three. Mo has started watching from his shop window.
Did he say it back? He didn't say it back. Okay. Tomorrow.
Mo is invested.
And Ana is nervous every single morning. Most of us would be. We expect chatting with strangers to be awkward.
But when researchers asked train commuters to chat with a stranger, they enjoyed the ride more. Even though almost everyone predicted the opposite.
And tiny chats count. Even a short, warm chat with a barista left people in a better mood than rushing.
One soup, one sandwich, and how's your mum?
Better! Thanks, Mo.
Theo sees that. And on day seven...
...Hey.
One word! Ana manages not to scream.
Day ten. Hey. Day twelve. Hey. Day fourteen...
He doesn't like me. I'm the annoying hello lady.
And this is exactly where most of us would quit. So let's check that calendar. Day fifteen. Night.
Every hello. Circled.
She remembered my name today.
Ana thinks she's annoying. Theo thinks she's the best part of his day. That's the liking gap. After we talk to someone, we tend to underestimate how much they liked us.
That short hey wasn't a door closing. It was a door that was stuck.
Day sixteen. Rain. The bench is empty. Day seventeen. Still empty.
Huh. I actually miss him.
Turns out, the hellos had become the best part of Ana's morning too.
She almost doesn't go. What if it's weird? But studies find that when we reach out to someone, they appreciate it a lot more than we expect.
Take the soup. Soup is never weird.
You... noticed I was gone?
Of course I noticed.
After that, the hellos get longer. A question. A story about the seagull. An actual laugh.

Quick reality check, though. One study estimated it takes roughly fifty hours together to become casual friends. By day twenty-nine, Ana and Theo are at about three. Not best friends. And that's okay. Friendship isn't one big moment. It's hours, stacked up.
So if you're the Ana in your story, the second hello matters more than the first. And they probably like you more than you think.
And if you're the Theo, that guarded feeling isn't a flaw. It's your brain protecting you. One word back is enough.
Day thirty. Ana walks to the bench... and Theo isn't there.
He's across the square. Next to Finn. Finn, who's been sitting alone all week.
Morning. I'm Theo.
Thirty days ago, Theo couldn't look up. Today, he's somebody's day one.
Maybe you're somebody's Ana.
